summary:
Same-sex activity is legal in Panama, and the sources reviewed record no criminal provision directed at transgender people.

Legal gender recognition is available but requires surgery, and no nonbinary recognition exists.

No Panamanian statute prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. The National Assembly blocked an amendment to the general anti-discrimination law in 2024, with the block defended on the argument that the existing text already covers the ground implicitly. A 2015 bill to ban discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity has not advanced. No act is recognised as a hate crime, so violence motivated by a victim's gender identity or orientation is not charged or recorded as such.

At the 2025 Universal Periodic Review, multiple states urged Panama to adopt explicit anti-discrimination protections, reform gender recognition, and strengthen safeguards against violence. The reforms remain stalled, and Panama's legal position lags much of Latin America.

Partner recognition is closed. Article 40 of the Code of Private International Law, approved on 8 May 2014, states that same-sex marriages are strictly prohibited and that foreign same-sex marriages will not be recognised. The Supreme Court ruled on 27 March 2023, after a seven-year delay, that the constitution confers no positive right to same-sex marriage. A constitutional amendment defining marriage as between a man and a woman was approved by the National Assembly on 29 October 2019 and withdrawn before the referendum following public protests. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under Panamanian law has no route to recognition, and no civil-union alternative is in force.

Public opinion data: a 2017 survey found 78% of Panamanians opposed to same-sex marriage; AmericasBarometer in 2023 recorded 12% approval, ranking Panama 18th of 22 countries surveyed in the Americas.

In the indigenous territory of Guna Yala, an Omeggid third-gender community is described as accepted as completely normal, with matriarchal figures holding elevated status. That is one local data point on how gender diversity is received; it does not describe the country as a whole.
tangentialFactors:
Marriage litigation ran for years without producing a right. Two suits, one seeking recognition of a marriage performed abroad and one challenging the family code directly, were combined after oral arguments in summer 2017, with amicus briefs from regional marriage-equality advocates and public support from the First Lady, against opposition led by Catholic and evangelical groups. In October 2017 Justice Luis Ramón Fábrega circulated a draft ruling holding the family code's marriage bars not unconstitutional and leaving civil unions to the National Assembly; he withdrew the draft in February 2018, and the government signalled it would comply with the Inter-American Court of Human Rights decision of 9 January 2018.

The Roman Catholic Church defeated a 2004 civil-union proposal and condemned the 2018 Inter-American Court advisory opinion, which one deputy called "a danger to the human race".
localsOnly:
Residents face restrictions that do not apply to a short-stay visitor. Gay and bisexual men are barred from donating blood under an indefinite deferral. Conversion therapy is not banned. No employment or housing discrimination protections exist on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, so a trans resident has no statutory remedy against a discriminatory landlord or employer.

Article 39 of the Constitution, which bars associations contrary to moral or legal order, has been used to refuse registration of gay organisations. The first such group, AHMNP, founded in 1996, gained legal recognition only in 2005 after a three-year battle.

Intersex surgery on infants is not prohibited, and the state has not regulated the practice.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not document how Panamanian border or immigration officers handle a passport whose gender marker differs from the holder's presentation, and no record of screening, secondary inspection or detention on that basis was located, nor any documented pattern of police targeting transgender people. The absence of a documented practice is not evidence that none occurs.

No Panamanian statute governing bathroom, changing-room or other single-sex facility access by gender identity was located in the sources reviewed.

The practical effect of the surgery requirement on a resident's ability to obtain a corrected identity document, and the processing time involved, are not sourced.

Whether the 2024 blocked anti-discrimination amendment will be reintroduced, and whether the 2023 Supreme Court ruling leaves any pending marriage case alive, are unresolved.
